doc.title: Pete Levin interviewed by Monk Rowe, Danbury, Connecticut, November 20, 2001

title: Whether he still plays the horn, and the Danbury brass quintet
summary: Levin plays horn very little now but describes an informal brass quintet in Danbury with Alan Raph and Bucky Milan.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: Do you still play the horn?

Very little. I have it, but it’s not something you can not touch for six months and just pick up. For a little while I was playing in a brass quintet a few years ago, up here in Danbury, just with some friends. It was a very relaxed situation. Actually Alan Raph, who you interviewed, was in that, and a local trumpet player, Bucky Milan who I’ve known for years, he played with Urbie Green and Buddy Rich years ago and he’s mainly an artist nowadays, paints beautifully. This was a very informal quintet, playing classical stuff. But nobody was playing their primary instrument. Alan wanted to play tuba, which he likes very much, and let’s see the trombone player was actually a trumpet player but he loved baritone horn. So he was playing the trombone parts on baritone horn. And Bucky was really an artist, and the second trumpet player I think was a student and she was very serious and very much into it, but the rest of us were well let’s have a couple of beers and play some brass music. And I was in a state where I was great for fifteen minutes and then my chops would start to go and then I couldn’t do anything after an hour. So I would © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
be lobbying to — let’s stop and have a beer, let’s take a long break. Long answer to an easy question. So no, I don’t play much. You can’t, you really have to keep up with that.
